chapters.title: Chapter 4: Tax and Rules in India

lessons.title: How ESOPs Are Taxed in India: Perquisite Tax at Exercise and Capital Gains at Sale

children.text: ESOPs are taxed twice, at two different moments, at two different rates, under two different heads of income. Almost every expensive ESOP mistake in India comes from not knowing that sentence.
This lesson works through both stages with one grant, for a listed company and an unlisted one, so you can see exactly where the money goes.

body.text: Stage one taxes the discount you received, as salary, on the day you exercise. Stage two taxes the growth after that, as capital gains, on the day you sell. Get the dividing line right and the rest is arithmetic.

children.text: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the
perquisite

sits in Section 17(1)(d) [Section 17(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961], and the valuation rule in Section 17(5)(h). The capital gains provisions are Section 196 [Section 111A], Section 197 [Section 112] and Section 198 [Section 112A]. The section numbers changed; the logic did not.

markDefs.definition: A benefit received from employment that is taxed as salary. The discount on shares received through an ESOP is one.

children.text: Stage One: The Perquisite at Exercise

body.latex: \text{Perquisite} = (\text{FMV on exercise date} - \text{Amount paid by employee}) \times \text{Shares}
body.caption: Added to your salary income for the year and taxed at your slab rate.

children.text: Nikhil exercises 2,000 options at an exercise price of ₹50 when the fair market value is ₹300. His perquisite is ₹5,00,000. At a 30% slab with 4% cess, so 31.2%, the tax is ₹1,56,000, and his employer deducts it as TDS. He has also paid ₹1,00,000 to exercise.

body.text: The perquisite is taxed whether or not you sell a single share. This is why an unlisted company exercise can leave you with a tax bill and no cash, a point worth planning for months in advance.

body.title: Compute the Perquisite
body.prompt: 2,000 options, exercise price ₹50, fair market value on the exercise date ₹300. What is the perquisite added to salary income?
body.explanation: (₹300 minus ₹50) × 2,000 = ₹5,00,000. At a 31.2% effective rate that is ₹1,56,000 of tax, deducted by the employer from salary.

children.text: Stage Two: Capital Gains at Sale
Here is the detail people get wrong most often. Your
cost of acquisition

is not what you paid to exercise. It is the fair market value that was already taxed as a perquisite. Section 73 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 49(2AA) of the 1961 Act] says so explicitly, and it exists to stop the same gain being taxed twice.

markDefs.definition: The value your capital gain is measured from. For ESOP shares it is the FMV already taxed as a perquisite, not the exercise price you paid.

body.title: What Is the Cost of Acquisition?
body.question: Nikhil paid ₹50 per share to exercise, when the FMV was ₹300. He later sells at ₹450. What figure does he deduct as cost of acquisition when computing his capital gain?
options: ₹300, the FMV already taxed as a perquisite
₹350, the exercise price plus the perquisite per share
Nil, since the shares came from his employer
body.explanation: The ₹250 per share gap was already taxed as salary at exercise. Taking ₹300 as the cost of acquisition means only the growth after that point, ₹150 a share, is taxed again as capital gains. Using ₹50 would tax the same ₹250 twice.

children.text: Holding period decides the rate
The
holding period
runs from the date the shares are allotted to you, not from the grant date or the vesting date.

markDefs.definition: The time between allotment of the shares and their sale, which decides whether a gain is short term or long term.

body.title: Listed vs unlisted shares at the sale stage

columns.label: Listed shares, sold on an exchange
points: Long term after more than 12 months
Long term gains taxed at 12.5%, with the first ₹1.25 lakh of eligible gains exempt each year
Securities transaction tax applies on the sale

columns.label: Unlisted shares
points: Long term only after more than 24 months
Long term gains taxed at 12.5%, with no annual exemption and no indexation
Short term gains added to income and taxed at your slab rate
No securities transaction tax, and no concessional short term rate

body.text: The gap that matters most is short term on unlisted shares. The same gain can be taxed at 12.5% or at your full slab rate depending on whether you crossed 24 months. For a large holding, a few weeks of patience can be worth lakhs.

body.title: Tax the Long Term Gain
body.prompt: Nikhil’s shares are listed and he sells after 14 months, making a capital gain of ₹3,00,000. Applying the 12.5% long term rate after the ₹1,25,000 annual exemption, and ignoring cess and surcharge, what is his capital gains tax?
body.explanation: ₹3,00,000 minus the ₹1,25,000 exemption leaves ₹1,75,000. At 12.5% that is ₹21,875. Had the shares been unlisted and sold at 20 months, the whole gain would have been short term and taxed at his slab rate, roughly ₹93,600.

body.title: The Threshold That Trips People Up
body.textWithBlank: Unlisted shares must be held for more than ___ months before a gain on sale is treated as long term.
body.explanation: Listed equity turns long term after 12 months, but unlisted shares need more than 24. Employees who exercise privately and sell in a buyback at month 20 are often surprised to find the gain taxed at their slab rate.

children.text: A falling share price after exercise.

You are taxed on the perquisite at the exercise date FMV, and that tax does not come back if the share later falls. If you then sell below that FMV, you book a capital loss, which can be set off against other capital gains under the rules, but not against your salary income. Exercising at a peak and selling in a trough is the worst of both worlds.
Shares of a foreign parent.

If you hold RSUs or options of an overseas parent company, the perquisite works the same way, but the shares are not listed on an Indian exchange, so the concessional listed equity rates do not apply and the 24-month test is the one that matters. There are also foreign asset reporting obligations in your return.

body.title: The Buyback Is in Month Twenty
body.scenario: Aisha exercised 6,000 options in an unlisted company 20 months ago, at an exercise price of ₹30 when the FMV was ₹180, and paid perquisite tax then. The company has now announced a buyback at ₹420, open for the next six weeks. A colleague tells her to wait for the next buyback so the gain becomes long term.
body.prompt: What are the numbers, and is waiting the right call?
body.modelAnswer: Her gain would be 6,000 × (₹420 minus ₹180) = ₹14,40,000, measured from the FMV taxed at exercise, not from her ₹30 exercise price. Selling now, at month 20, means the gain is short term for unlisted shares and taxed at her slab rate, roughly ₹4,49,280 at 31.2%. Waiting past 24 months would make it long term at 12.5%, about ₹1,80,000, a difference of roughly ₹2,69,280. That is a real saving, but it assumes a second buyback happens, at a price at least as good, within a reasonable time. Given that buyback windows are discretionary and capped, the sensible approach is to weigh a certain ₹14,40,000 gain today against an uncertain window later, and consider selling part now if she needs the money or the concentration risk is uncomfortable. Tax should inform the decision, not drive it.

points: ESOPs are taxed twice: as a salary perquisite at exercise, and as capital gains at sale.
The perquisite is FMV on the exercise date minus what you paid, taxed at your slab rate, with TDS deducted by your employer.
Your cost of acquisition at sale is the FMV already taxed at exercise, not your exercise price. Using the exercise price taxes the same money twice.
Listed shares turn long term after 12 months; unlisted shares need more than 24.
The same ₹3,00,000 gain cost ₹21,875 as a listed long term gain and ₹93,600 as an unlisted short term one.
Perquisite tax is not refunded if the share price falls afterwards, and the later loss is a capital loss that cannot be set against salary.
Shares of a foreign parent do not get the concessional listed equity rates, and carry foreign asset reporting obligations.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Rates and thresholds used here reflect the position as described in the sources cited for this course, assume a 30% slab with 4% cess, and ignore surcharge, which matters at higher incomes. Tax law changes with every Union Budget, so confirm the current position with a qualified professional before acting.
